reference.source: ATS/ERS statements on eosinophilic lung disease / Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
clinicalPearls: A subacute to chronic illness over weeks to months with cough, breathlessness, fever, night sweats, and weight loss, more common in middle-aged women and often in those with asthma or atopy
The classic radiographic hallmark is peripheral, upper-zone predominant consolidation described as the 'photographic negative of pulmonary oedema'
Marked peripheral blood eosinophilia is usual, and bronchoalveolar lavage shows prominent eosinophilia
Serum IgE is often elevated and inflammatory markers are raised
It responds rapidly to corticosteroids, frequently with improvement within days, but relapse on withdrawal or dose reduction is very common
Many patients require prolonged corticosteroid therapy, and asthma frequently coexists or emerges over the course
Consider eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis when there is asthma with extrapulmonary features such as neuropathy or vasculitis
Exclude drug reactions and parasitic infection as secondary causes of pulmonary eosinophilia
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia is characterised by sustained accumulation of eosinophils within the alveoli and interstitium, driven by eosinophil-active cytokines and chemokines in a background that is often atopic or asthmatic. Persistent eosinophil infiltration and release of cytotoxic granule proteins produce dense alveolar filling, predominantly in the peripheral and upper lung zones, giving the characteristic reverse-oedema distribution. The inflammation is corticosteroid sensitive but tends to recur, and prolonged uncontrolled disease can occasionally lead to fibrotic change.
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution CT showing peripheral, upper-zone predominant consolidation and ground-glass opacity
Full blood count demonstrating peripheral eosinophilia and bronchoalveolar lavage confirming alveolar eosinophilia
ANCA testing and assessment for extrapulmonary features to evaluate for eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis
Stool examination and serology for parasites, and review of drug history
Pulmonary function tests, which may show restrictive or obstructive patterns, and spirometry for coexisting asthma
redFlags: Extrapulmonary features such as mononeuritis multiplex, cardiac or renal involvement suggesting systemic vasculitis
Frequent relapse or steroid dependence requiring steroid-sparing therapy
Progressive breathlessness or hypoxaemia despite treatment
Very high eosinophil counts raising concern for hypereosinophilic syndrome
reference.prognosis: The response to corticosteroids is usually excellent and rapid, but relapse is frequent when treatment is reduced or stopped, so many patients need prolonged therapy; long-term outcome is generally good provided disease is controlled.
pitfalls: Failing to recognise the peripheral photographic-negative-of-oedema pattern on imaging
Stopping corticosteroids too early and provoking relapse
Missing an evolving eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis when systemic features appear
Not excluding drug and parasitic causes of pulmonary eosinophilia
